newsitem.title: USA: Children smuggled into U.S. may be part of trend.
newsitem.headline: Children smuggled into U.S. may be part of trend.

text.p: A nationwide alert has been issued for 10 children aged four to 14 who entered the United States on illegal passports and are now missing, officials say.

Authorities have no concrete information on why the children, believed to be Hispanic, were brought to the United States, although theories include a possible adoption ring. But they say the case reflects what may be a rising trend.

"We have seen an increase in the United States of spurious travel documents to facilitate movement of children, whether for serious criminal offences like pedophilia or to achieve family reunification" in contentious divorce cases, said John Davis, a special agent with the State Department's diplomatic security service.

An alert for the 10 children, including pictures, has been broadcast at the request of the diplomatic security service to law enforcement agencies in 49 states by the Virginia-based National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children.

Elizabeth Yore, director of the center's international division, said she is not sure if there are more instances of children being brought illegally into the United States or if media attention has heightened awareness.
But the international law enforcement community is more focused on the subject and her organisation has begun to get more inquiries from overseas, she said.

Recently, Yore said, the centre has heard from some parents in poor foreign countries who said they gave their children to certain people, believing the children would be brought to the United States for medical care, but then never heard from them again.

She said none of those inquiries concerned the 10 youths involved in the case of Theresa Martinez, a 34-year-old Bolivian woman, who was arrested at her Gaithersberg, Maryland, home and charged by federal authorities with being the "ringleader of a sophisticated false identity document vendor operation."
Seven other suspects, who allegedly obtained passports with fraudulent birth certificates, were also arrested and other arrests are expected, authorities said.

Authorities said Martinez, who has three children of her own and used several aliases, applied fraudulently for the U.S. passports with birth certificates she manufactured. At least 24 passports were obtained in this way, Davis said.
Officials say that travel document fraud, once considered a "soft crime," has increasingly become a primary tool for frustrating international crime of all kinds.

That is how authorities caught Marvin Hersh, a Florida University professor, who was arrested April 11 in a separate case on charges of illegally smuggling a 17-year-old Honduran boy to the United States. A U.S. magistrate in Florida kept Hersh in jail saying he was "driven by pedophilia."
